chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
title: Playing Afro-Cuban jazz and tipica without conflict
summary: Machito says Afro-Cuban jazz opened a new market without hurting tipica fans; both were played, sometimes in the same dance, on clave.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: They didn't confuse you, did they?

In other words, here is Machito playing Afro-Cuban jazz, in jazz clubs and here you are doing something on a typical music front which was also okay. Did both rhythms, popularity of both rhythms - Were you able to live with both or did one hurt you?
No one hurt me. The Afro-Cuban jazz helped us to get into a market.
And it didn't turn off the typical Latin music lovers?

No, no, no, it was another market and people sometime respect the versatility or creativity, whatever you want to call it, and we were lucky that we had the element' to be in both sides where the jazz people respect us and the typica people respect us, because we never confused what we was playing. Afro-Cuban jazz was Afro-Cuban jazz. When we was playing tipico, we played tipico and, as a matter of fact, sometimes we combined. In the same dance we played four or five tipica numbers and then we played Afro-jazz thing that was danceable .....

...... because always our music's been danceable. No matter how fast, how slow or whatever. Is in clave especially for the people that know how to dance, especially American people. They learned correctly how to dance, so we didn't have problems.
